analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas drilling leases off Southern California's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee after a single subcommittee hearing and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from issuing any new lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in the Southern California planning area of the Outer Continental Shelf, the federal waters off Southern California's coast. In practice, it would lock out new offshore drilling in that zone under any future administration, regardless of what leasing plans the Interior Department adopts. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and received one subcommittee hearing before the Congress ended without any committee vote or floor action.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, beachgoers, and people whose jobs and property depend on an oil-spill-free coastline in Southern California. A permanent leasing ban reduces the risk of offshore spills like the 1969 Santa Barbara blowout that fouled the region's beaches, protects coastal tourism and fishing economies, and keeps billions of barrels' worth of federal waters from being opened to drilling. It also benefits the climate by keeping new oil and gas reserves from being developed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Southern California coastal communities and beach economies

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to prohibit the Secretary of the Interior from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil or natural gas in the Southern California planning area, overriding any other provision of law.

Because the prohibition is written into statute 'notwithstanding any other provision of this section or any other law,' it would bind future administrations, not just the leasing program in effect today.
The bill covers any subsequent oil and gas leasing program developed under the Act, so new drilling could not return through a future five-year leasing plan.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies and their suppliers, who would be permanently shut out of new leasing in the Southern California planning area, and the federal Treasury, which forgoes potential bonus bids, rents, and royalties from any leases that might otherwise have been sold there. Energy consumers are unaffected in any near-term way, since the area has seen little new leasing activity.

drawbacks.text: A permanent statutory ban forfeits federal royalty revenue and bonus payments that new leases in the region could have generated for the Treasury, and removes potential domestic energy supply from future planning.

The bill was a single-issue prohibition with no hearing record in the provided materials beyond one subcommittee session, so its regional economic effects were never fully aired in committee or on the floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a permanent legal shield against new drilling off Southern California's populated coast, which is where spill risk falls on ordinary people, their beaches, and their livelihoods. The cost is foregone federal leasing revenue and forgone energy supply, which are real but modest given how little activity the area has attracted. On balance the trade favors coastal residents, but the bill never got far enough for anyone to test that argument in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, sent to a subcommittee, got one hearing, and then the Congress ended without a committee vote or floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Levin (D-CA) introduced the bill on May 7, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On May 12, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and on May 13, 2021, the subcommittee held a hearing on it.
No further action was taken: the committee never voted the bill out, the House never debated it, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill dead.
Support was limited to the sponsor and 13 cosponsors, all House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The offshore oil and gas industry is better off, because the federal waters off Southern California remain legally open to future leasing rather than closed by statute; so is any future administration that wants the option to offer leases there. Coastal communities gained nothing beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The offshore drilling industry and future administrations

for.name: Rep. Mike Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 7, 2021, to permanently bar oil and gas leasing off Southern California.

for.name: 13 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all of its support in the chamber came from Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and never brought it to a committee vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 members behind the bill were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it, but the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar new federal leases for exploration, development, and production in the Southern California planning area, shutting the industry out of that zone. Its interest in keeping the area open runs against coastal residents, whose beaches and economies absorb the spill risk.

industries.industry: Southern California coastal tourism and fishing
industries.note: A permanent leasing ban lowers the risk of an offshore oil spill damaging beaches, fisheries, and the tourism economy that coastal jobs depend on.
